'''Louis John Lanzerotti''' (born April 16, 1938) is an American physicist. He is a Distinguished Research Professor of [[physics]] in the ''Center for Solar-Terrestrial Research'' at [[New Jersey Institute of Technology]] (NJIT) in [[Newark, New Jersey]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LhdTAAAAMAAJ|title=IEEE Membership Directory|date=2001-01-01|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://physics.njit.edu/people/research-professors.php|title=NJIT: Physics: Research Professors|accessdate=2016-06-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160618160247/http://physics.njit.edu/people/research-professors.php|archive-date=2016-06-18|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://centers.njit.edu/cstr/ |title=Center for Solar-Terrestrial Research Welcome!|publisher=NJIT |accessdate=2018-01-05}}</ref>

His principal research interests have included space plasmas, geophysics, and engineering problems related to the impacts of atmospheric and space processes and the space environment on space and terrestrial technologies.

==Early life==
Louis J. Lanzerotti was born and grew up in [[Carlinville, Illinois]]. He earned a BS in Engineering Physics in 1960 from [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]]. He obtained his MS and PhD degrees, both in Physics, and both from [[Harvard University]] in 1963 and 1965 respectively.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/aip/governing-board/louis-j-lanzerotti|title=Louis J. Lanzerotti {{!}} American Institute of Physics|website=www.aip.org|date=7 February 2014|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref>

==Career==
After serving as a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University, he joined AT&T's [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]] in 1965 to engage in engineering and scientific research on Earth's radiation belts, the existence of which was confirmed a few years earlier by [[James Van Allen]]. AT&T's [[Telstar]] satellites had recently been launched, providing Lanzerotti and his colleagues with data for analyzing and interpreting the radiation belts and their effects of radiation on space systems. This marked the beginning of Lanzerotti’s leadership in the field now called "[[space weather]]".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://honors.agu.org/winners/louis-j-lanzerotti/|title=Louis J. Lanzerotti. American Geophysical Union. 2011 William Bowie Medal Winner.|date=2011-08-02|language=en-US|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref> Lanzerotti's work led to him being named a ''Distinguished Member of Technical Staff'' at [[Lucent Technologies]].

Lanzerotti worked with multiple satellite programs and space missions, including the [[ATS-1]] and [[ATS-3]] communications satellites, the interplanetary IMP 4 and IMP 5 [[Explorers program|explorer missions]], the [[Voyager program|Voyager missions]] to the outer planets and interstellar medium, the [[Advanced Composition Explorer]] solar wind mission, and the [[Cassini–Huygens|Cassini mission]] to Saturn. Furthermore, Lanzerotti has been awarded many National Science Foundation research grants<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/advancedSearchResult?PIId=&PIFirstName=&PILastName=lanzerotti&IncludeCoPI=true&PIOrganization=&PIState=&PIZip=&PICountry=&ProgOrganization=&ProgEleCode=&BooleanElement=All&ProgRefCode=&BooleanRef=All&Program=&ProgOfficer=&Keyword=&AwardNumberOperator=&AwardAmount=&AwardInstrument=&ActiveAwards=true&ExpiredAwards=true&OriginalAwardDateOperator=&StartDateOperator=&ExpDateOperator=|title=NSF Award Search: Lanzerotti|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref> including as the [[principal investigator]] for instruments aboard the [[Ulysses (spacecraft)|Ulysses mission]] over the poles of the Sun, the [[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo mission]] to Jupiter, and more recently the [[Van Allen Probes]], launched in 2012 to study Earth's radiation belts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://honors.agu.org/winners/louis-j-lanzerotti/|title=Louis J. Lanzerotti|date=2011-08-02|website=American Geophysical Union|language=en-US|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref> He retired in 2002 and remained a consultant to Alcatel-Lucent through 2008. In 2002, he was appointed a Distinguished Research Professor of Physics in the Center for Solar-Terrestrial Research at the New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark, New Jersey. He has also served as an adjunct professor of electrical engineering at the University of Florida and as a Regents' lecture at University of California, Los Angeles. He is currently ''Distinguished Research Professor of Physics'' at the [[New Jersey Institute of Technology]].

Much of his research has involved close collaborations with telecommunications service providers on commercial satellite and long-haul (principally transoceanic) cables. His research has also involved geomagnetism, solid earth geophysics, and some oceanography. This research has been applied to design and operations of systems associated with spacecraft and cable operations. Lanzerotti has served as principal investigator or co-investigator on several United States NASA interplanetary and planetary missions including ATS-1&3, IMP-4&5, Voyager 1&2, Ulysses, Galileo Orbiter and Entry Probe, ACE, and Cassini. Currently, he is a Principal Investigator with instruments on each of the two spacecraft in the NASA Van Allen Probes mission launched August 2012. He has also conducted geophysical research in the Antarctic and the Arctic beginning in the 1970s, directed largely toward understanding of Earth's upper atmosphere and space environments.

Lanzerotti has served as an associate editor for the [[Journal of Geophysical Research]] and is the founding editor of the  online journal [http://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/agu/journal/10.1002/(ISSN)1542-7390/ Space Weather].

In recognition of his career as a research scientist and engineer, Lanzerotti was appointed by US President [[George W. Bush]] to the [[National Science Board]], the 24-member governing body of the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF)<ref>"NJIT : Bush Nominates NJIT Space Explorer Louis Lanzerotti To NSF Governing Board"</ref> and served a 6-year term from 2004 to 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/members/former.jsp|title=National Science Board|website=National Science Board. Former Members.|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref> He served on the board as a ''Board Consultant'' from May 2010 until April 2012. Lanzerotti also led a 12-member panel organized by the [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] (NRC) of the [[National Academies]] to identify possible causes of unintended acceleration in vehicles in the aftermath of [[Toyota]]'s large automobile recalls.

Lanzerotti has authored or co-authored of more than 500 refereed publications, contributing to research that includes studies of space plasmas and geophysics, and engineering problems related to the impact of atmospheric and space processes (a.k.a. "[[space weather]]") on terrestrial and spaceborne technologies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aip.org/aip/governing-board/louis-j-lanzerotti|title=Louis J. Lanzerotti {{!}} American Institute of Physics|website=www.aip.org|date=7 February 2014|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref>  Lanzerotti co-authored a book on [[radiation belt]] physics <ref>{{Cite book|bibcode=1974pdrb.book.....S|title=Particle diffusion in the radiation belts|last1=Schulz|first1=Michael|last2=Lanzerotti|first2=Louis J.|date=1974-01-01}}</ref> and has co-edited four books. He has eight patents issued or filed.

In addition to his career in science, Lanzerotti served in the [[Harding Township, New Jersey]] local government.  In the 1980s he was elected to three 3-year terms on his Harding Township school board, with 6 years as chair of its curriculum committee and 6 years as vice president. Since 1993 he has served six elected terms on the township governing body, including 3 years as mayor.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://honors.agu.org/winners/louis-j-lanzerotti/|title=Louis J. Lanzerotti|date=2011-08-02|language=en-US|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dailyrecord.com/story/news/local/morris-county/government/2015/01/11/new-mayors-council-members-sworn/21522781/|title=Morris County: New mayors, council members sworn in for 2015|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Louis Lanzerotti married Mary Yvonne DeWolf Lanzerotti, Ph.D., on June 19, 1965, in St. Paul's Church, Cambridge, Massachusetts. They have two children, Mary Yvonne Lanzerotti, Ph.D. and Louis DeWolf Lanzerotti, Ph.D.<ref>Personal conversation with Louis John Lanzerotti, September 5, 2026.</ref>
